item.title: Microsoft’s Global Outage and Fixes: What We Know
item.description:
Microsoft is reporting widespread improvements to its services after a global outage took them offline on Thursday, disrupting communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world. The company, headquartered in Redmond, Wash., said on Friday that it was seeing “encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure.”

“We remain focused on addressing residual impact and ensuring reliable service restoration,” the company added.

Here’s what to know as of Friday afternoon.

Outages started disrupting Microsoft tools and apps around noon Eastern time on Thursday and quickly spread to more than 70 countries and territories, affecting millions of users, according to Downdetector, an outage-tracking site.

Some of Microsoft’s most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, stopped working.

Microsoft said in a statement on Friday that “for now, we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” It added that the problem was “a technical issue not related to cyber or A.I.” agents.

The company has yet to provide a clear answer, although it has promised to make public a full report that identifies the “root cause” of the outage.

In statements on Thursday and Friday, it provided some details.

Microsoft said on Thursday that “a portion of infrastructure” was experiencing “elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” That could mean that increased stress on its network was caused by a “number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company said.

Microsoft said the servers were failing health checks — periodic, automated assessments that ensure they are functioning correctly and efficiently. It said the failed health checks “may originate from a specific component that’s responsible for processing server health.”

On Friday, Microsoft said the problem had been introduced to the system “during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.” It said it had addressed the underlying issue, allowing its tools and apps to begin to function normally again.

“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” it said. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

Luca Arnaboldi, an assistant professor of cybersecurity at the School of Computer Science at the University of Birmingham in England, said the outage was a reminder that when people use “the cloud,” they are actually relying on servers, which have finite resources.

“In this particular case, as servers became unavailable, capacity on the remaining servers increased, leaving fewer machines to handle the traffic,” he said in a statement. Even after some of the original servers came back online, he added, “the ones currently under strain now fail, creating a constant catch-up.”

Parents struggled to contact their children’s schools, some government services faltered and many office workers could not access email.

The outage affected parts of the federal government, including the U.S. House of Representatives, according to Samantha Carter, a spokeswoman for the office that oversees House operations.

“We have seen improvements to Outlook’s functionality this morning, but will continue to monitor the situation until all issues are resolved and full functionality is restored to all Microsoft applications,” Ms. Carter said in an email on Friday.

Elsewhere in the world, Britain’s National Health Service said the outage was having a “disruptive impact.” The National Pharmacy Association of Britain said the issues at the N.H.S. were making it difficult for pharmacies to communicate with doctors and some patients, which could cause delays in filling prescriptions. The Metropolitan Police in London said its online contact forms weren’t working.

In Australia, intelligence and police forces said that their operations had been affected. Singapore told taxpayers that email had been disrupted, and the Supreme Court of the Philippines and the European Court of Human Rights said the outage could cause delays in its work.

Reporting was contributed by Isabella Kwai, Karla Adam and Adeel Hassan.

item.title: How Does a 74-Year-Old in Argentina Escape House Arrest on the Fifth Floor?
item.description:
Time was running out for Leonardo Bertulazzi. After decades of safe harbor in Argentina, Mr. Bertulazzi, a former member of a far-left militant group that kidnapped and murdered Italy’s prime minister in 1978, faced imminent extradition back to Italy.

In Europe, a 27-year prison sentence for terrorism-related crimes awaited Mr. Bertulazzi, according to Argentina’s defense ministry.

Mr. Bertulazzi, 74, was placed in house arrest. The police were stationed across the street from the 5th-floor apartment he shared with his wife in Buenos Aires, Argentina’s capital. He’d had three strokes in the last two years, his lawyer said, and he was forced to wear an ankle monitor.

None of that seemed to stop Mr. Bertulazzi from planning his escape.

On Tuesday, while much of the Buenos Aires’ law enforcement apparatus was focused on the visit by Pope Leo, two police officers checked on Mr. Bertulazzi during a routine shift change, according to an official with knowledge of an investigation into Mr. Bertulazzi’s flight who was not authorized to speak publicly.

But this time, when the officers rang the apartment’s doorbell, nobody answered. Investigators believe Mr. Bertulazzi had escaped between 6 a.m. and 8 a.m. that morning.

Mr. Bertulazzi’s ankle monitor still showed he was at the apartment, the official said. A search revealed a metal box holding a mess of wires plugged into an outlet, prompting the officers to call an explosives disposal unit, according to the official.

Argentina’s defense ministry said Mr. Bertulazzi was charged with possessing explosives in connection with his activities with the Red Brigades, the Italian terrorist group that in 1978 kidnapped and assassinated Aldo Moro, the Italian prime minister at the time.

After the all-clear, officers opened the box and found the monitor wrapped around a plastic tube, the official said, which had been coated in animal fat to trick moisture sensors and stuffed with a type of heating pad often used for back pain — creating a contraption that approximated a human leg.

At the fifth-floor window, officers found climbing ropes and a harness, the official with knowledge of the investigation said, adding that Mr. Bertulazzi had rappelled down to a second-floor terrace on another property before running across rooftops, crossing through an empty lot and climbing over a gate.

Closed-circuit footage, shared in local media and confirmed by the official, showed a man dressed in dark clothes tumbling over the side of a green metal fence on a cobblestone street. In the footage, the white-haired figure slammed onto the pavement, stood up and took a moment to rest, leaning against a wall and limping around.

His lawyer, who had argued that his client’s health was too poor for him to withstand prison in Italy, said escape was a natural choice for Mr. Bertulazzi. “Given his age and health condition, honestly, I understand him,” said the lawyer, Rodolfo Yanzon.

Days later, Argentine authorities are still searching for Mr. Bertulazzi. The defense ministry has offered a reward of 20 million pesos, or about $13,000, for information that leads to his recapture. If captured, Mr. Yanzon said, Mr. Bertulazzi would likely be charged with evading justice and placed in jail pending extradition.

Mr. Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades, a Marxist-Leninist paramilitary organization that conducted robberies, assaults and assassinations in the 1970s as part of a campaign to foment revolution in Italy. The group is most famous for kidnapping Mr. Moro in March 1978. The Red Brigades held him for nearly two months before fatally shooting him and leaving his body in a car trunk in Rome.

As a high-ranking member of the Red Brigades, Mr. Bertulazzi helped coordinate that kidnapping and others, Argentina’s national security ministry said in a statement in 2024.

The authorities first arrested Mr. Bertulazzi in Argentina in 2002. He was later released, and within two years he was granted refugee status and protections from extradition. But in 2024, Mr. Bertulazzi was arrested after the election of the current president, Javier Milei, a right-wing leader who promised tough-on-crime policies.

“This arrest reflects Argentina’s commitment to the values ​​of democracy and the rule of law, and demonstrates to the world its firm resolve not to tolerate unpunished murderers,” the security ministry’s 2024 statement said.

After a lengthy legal battle, courts this month had cleared the way for Mr. Bertulazzi to be extradited, as Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, had requested.

item.title: In Canada, Watching the N.H.L. Has Become Expensive and Cumbersome
item.description:
The National Hockey League season is less than two months old, and much of the focus in Canada has been on how expensive it is to attend games, and how costly and cumbersome it has become to watch them on television.

Attendance has fallen in several markets, including Edmonton, where Connor McDavid has an astonishing 49 points in 20 games and is on pace to challenge Wayne Gretzky’s single-season scoring record of 215 points.

This week, The Globe and Mail reported that three TV providers had filed a complaint with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission asking Rogers Sportsnet to reverse its decision to put more than 50 Monday night N.H.L. games behind a paywall on its streaming service for an extra $13 a month.

Further increasing the cost and complexity of watching hockey, Wednesday night games are on Prime Video. TSN broadcasts some regional games with blackouts, and a subscription to NHL Centre Ice is needed to watch out-of-market games.

Until this season, the N.H.L. could be found for free.

In June, the CBC and Rogers Sportsnet announced that the national broadcaster would no longer air N.H.L. games on Saturday nights, a first in 75 years, ending the cultural institution “Hockey Night in Canada.” Last month, the CBC announced it would begin airing Professional Women’s Hockey League games when its season begins in December.

When the news broke, we asked Canada Letter readers to send us their thoughts and memories of “Hockey Night.” The response was overwhelming, and we’d like to share some today. (Responses have been edited for length and clarity.)

“For my childhood in the '60s and ’70s, ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ wasn’t a TV show. It was Saturday night, the once a week chance to see an N.H.L. game on TV. One game. It might as well have been church. For my father and I, it was our greatest bonding experience. We could talk about the game together, watch the game together, anticipate the game — together. And hope for that ultimate fan prize: a bench-clearing brawl.” — Allen Gibson

“I grew up playing hockey in central New York state. When cable TV came to the area, the biggest selling point was that our cable network would carry a station from Kingston, Ontario. The only thing that I do remember clearly is that every Saturday night we watched ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ It was like winning the lottery every week.” — Brian Goldblatt

“I was born the day of the first ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ broadcast on Nov. 1, 1952. One of my first memories as a young boy is sitting with dad in the basement on Saturday night breathlessly waiting for Foster Hewitt’s voice and wondering what the score might be (the early broadcasts started mid-game). Hockey has been in my blood since then, and I am both blessed (1967!) and cursed (59 years!) by my support of the Maple Leafs. The demise of this CBC broadcast is the direct result of the fragmentation of sports broadcasting. I fear that this continuing trend may have the longer term effect of alienating fans. It has for me with hockey, after a lifetime of living with this beautiful game.” — John Butler

“This is shattering. I have just started to follow hockey, and watching these broadcasts has made me feel part of the hockey community more than anything else. So sick of the ESPN effect on sports — slick programming that makes every sporting event seem like every other sporting event. Canadians, and true hockey fans everywhere, should be outraged by this loss, and clamor to bring it back. Hockey’s roots in the Great North should be preserved.” — Doyla Rosati

“My best memory of ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ relates to the old theme song, by the late Dolores Claman. There was a time, not that long ago, when you could easily find other Canadians in an overseas airport just by whistling the first few notes of the theme. As if on cue, another Canadian would respond with the next notes. It was always a magical moment when traveling.” — Michael Olsen

“It is so depressing that corporate greed can wipe out one of the most iconic cultural traditions in Canada. Even though I’m not the biggest hockey fan, my family was. And every Saturday night growing up at home I’d hear the familiar opening tune of ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ It is one of my most heartwarming memories of watching my family around the TV cheering on the Leafs. To this day, that music comes on and it reminds me I’m part of that glorious Canadian tradition too. Especially at this time when celebrating Canadian pride is at its strongest in my lifetime.” — Alida Stevenson

“In the late 1980s we had a satellite dish (one of those big ones) while living in Colorado. We ended up watching a lot of CBC programming because it was free, including ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ I knew almost nothing about hockey. But I started watching from time to time, especially after the Quebec Nordiques came to Denver and became the Colorado Avalanche. ‘Hockey Night’ taught me about hockey enough that I could enjoy it.” — Karen Wydeven

“There are a lot of varied opinions on CBC’s role in Canada, however in this matter, I think many agree that it will be a very large loss, but also a possible turning point for our public broadcaster. I spent a lot of nights watching CBC’s ‘H.N.I.C.' or listening to CBC on the radio for the games. Hopefully CBC will take the opportunity to become the national broadcaster for the P.W.H.L., something I wish had been when I was a young girl. How incredible it would have been for 5-year-old me to have watched women play the sport I love so much. Something I now wish for younger female athletes.” — Tammy Jakeman

“As an avid fan during the Canadiens’ amazing run in the ’70s I wanted to watch ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ on Saturdays. My dad didn’t think it was appropriate for a teenage girl to be watching hockey. He didn’t know I listened to almost every game on the radio during the week. So I made a deal with him, I would crochet in front of the television if I could watch with him.” — Cremilda Dias

“I grew up in Montreal in a family that came from a small Greek island: Naxos. My grandfather came over in 1907 but we had quite a few relatives in the city who were recent immigrants and still struggled to speak either English or French. On Saturday nights we often went to family functions in the homes of relatives who hadn’t been in Canada that long and were still emotionally tied to the village. By 8 o’clock, the men would gather around the black and white TV to watch whatever game was on. None of them ever missed it, especially when they were together and the Montreal Canadiens were playing. They argued passionately about every play, every lost opportunity, the strength and weaknesses of each player, entirely in Greek. It seemed that as soon as they stepped off the boat and started their lives in Montreal they discovered ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ It became their doorway to their new country.” — Emmanuel Hadzipetros

“Born in 1960, I watched ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ growing up. I grew tired of the violence and watch it only occasionally during the season and playoffs. I am thrilled that the dropping of it will help promote more coverage of the women’s game.” — Susan Funnell

“As a farm kid growing up in small town southern Alberta in the early 1960s we had one station, CBC, and ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ was a Saturday night ritual. If the atmospheric gods were smiling on us, we were graced with a static filled black and white image, but at least the audio was good. To this day hearing the theme magically transports me back to small town Alberta surrounded by my brothers and sister and cold dark winter nights. It’s the end of an era.” — Laurence Torsher

“It represents a slice of Canadian culture that is only a slice, as the success of the P.W.H.L. shows. The negative effects of the male professional hockey machine are well-documented. I’m proud of how the CBC is a platform for less-popular sports, like women’s hockey and soccer, volleyball and softball, and the non-hockey Olympics. These athletes compete for a pittance and often have to support themselves on the side. I think it helps keep the ‘sport’ of it in perspective.” — Tim Dyck

“In 1969, overpacked car driven by my new French Canadian husband, we went from my family home in Connecticut to Montreal. I’d had Latin and Spanish in school and my husband had very little English. We met one year before in the German pub on the Expo Islands. Twelve months later, after long distance calls, torturous letters written and read with bilingual dictionaries, and two weeks of intensive French classes, we married. We lived in a three-story apartment in the middle unit with the French sounds of the neighbors’ radios seeping into the rooms. However, most of my French that year came from ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ We watched it at the grandparents’ where the large extended family gathered on Saturday evenings to cheer encouragement. I also learned a couple of cuss words when things did not go well.” — Carol Ann St-Jean

“I lived in Montreal during the war Vietnam War, and later Vancouver. What surprised me at the time, being a Yank with no interest in sports in general of any kind, how totally captivating ‘H.N.I.C.’ was for Canadians. Everyone, certainly among the Canadians I worked with and socialized with, was home watching hockey on telly that night, and talking about the games the following day. I also recall that crime stats dropped to almost zero on ‘H.N.I.C.’ days. The entire cultural spectacle was lost on me at the time, yet another indication of how little us Yanks knew and understood Canada at the time.” — Dick Matthews

“When I was growing up in Northern Ontario, ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ was two nights a week, both Wednesday and Saturday. On school nights I was allowed to watch one period, on Saturdays two. But each bedtime was the same. I would kneel by my bed and pray that the Leafs won, so my dad wouldn’t be sad.” — Rhonda Wright

“As a now-elderly American I first heard ‘H.N.I.C.’ on static filled radio under the covers when I should have been sleeping. As an adult in the Detroit suburbs, it came to me from CBC Windsor. For me it was and remained the gold standard in sports broadcasting. Whatever will replace it on Saturday night will fail to match the memories. We live in an age of change, and must adapt. But some changes we can regret, and this will sting, at least for awhile.” — Joe Sher

Shawna Richer is the Canada editor at The Times. She lives in Toronto and has been editing and writing about sports for more than 25 years.

By Mark Colley

Caleb Linton, 7, had a liver transplant at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children when he was 6 months old. The doctors, he says, saved his life. That’s why he’s here.

“Here” is a room in the old wing of SickKids, where Linton is performing this month in an adventurous theatrical production that unfolds across eight floors and more than a dozen rooms of the working hospital. The SickKids Foundation is staging the show, which features 16 professional actors and a rotating cast of former patients, to kick off a fund-raising initiative with a goal of 2.5 billion Canadian dollars.

Michael Rubinoff, who produced the hit musical “Come From Away” on Broadway and the West End, is behind the performance. He says this show is “the most profound experience I’ve had as a producer.” It is also among the most challenging.

Six separate audience groups move through different parts of the hospital while the story unfolds. Monica Dottor, playing a doctor, meets one group in a hallway, while PJ Prudat, dressed as a therapeutic clown, wheelies down the same hallway with another.

The choreography is orchestrated from a dark office tucked away on the sixth floor, where the stage manager Kate Sandeson watches video feeds from each room. She is one of six stage mangers on the production, more than the largest professional productions in Toronto, Rubinoff said.

A project this complex would normally take two years to put together. The creative team did it in six months. The Toronto director Mitchell Cushman, a co-creator, likened it to “building the airplane while you’re flying.”

The SickKids Foundation has raised about 1 billion Canadian dollars so far in its 10-year campaign, which began in 2023. “It’s a huge number,” said Jennifer Bernard, president and C.E.O. of the foundation, and it required an equally ambitious launch. She has seen the show 10 times.

Few members of the public, however, will get the chance. Most of the 21 performances, spread over three weeks for audiences of 100, are for donors and hospital staff members. Only one, on Nov. 20, is open to the public, and a lottery for one of 42 available pairs of tickets has drawn more than a thousand entries.

Mark Colley is a reporter for The Times based in Vancouver. He covers breaking news and Canada.

Trekking through the wilds of the Yukon territory, the American novelist Maggie Shipstead reconsiders her relationship to aging and risk.

Four grizzly bears were responsible for the attack that killed two women in British Columbia this month, wildlife authorities said this week. The sow and her three cubs were captured over the weekend, and forensic testing, including the examination of animal DNA, conclusively linked them to the attack.

Giant roadside attractions — like Tyra the Tyrannosaurus of Drumheller, Alberta — have helped put hundreds of communities on the map. What happens when their novelty fades and costs pile up?

Stormy weather that battered the Pacific Northwest and southwestern Canada spread during the week, bringing the region’s first major dose of winter rains.

How are we doing?We’re eager to have your thoughts about this newsletter and events in Canada in general. Please send them to nytcanada@nytimes.com.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
The Eurovision Song Contest will crown its first Asia champion in Bangkok on Saturday, in an event that will test whether a high-camp singing competition with an ardent fan base can appeal to audiences in a new market.

The inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia comprises artists and original songs from 11 countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. It will be live-streamed on YouTube at 8:30 p.m. local time (8:30 a.m. Eastern) and broadcast by television stations across the region.

Eurovision has been a fixture of the European cultural calendar since it began in 1956. Past winners include Sweden’s ABBA and the Canadian chanteuse Celine Dion, who represented Switzerland in 1988.

Asian artists have readily embraced the kitschy outfits and spectacular sets that are part of Eurovision tradition, with costumes that include traditional dress, as well as feathered capes and sequined corsets. Malaysia’s performer plans to enter the stage in a giant teardrop.

But the Eurovision format has not been tested in Asia. Fans and regional partners have expressed concern in recent weeks that budget constraints, production issues and weak audience demand could imperil the spinoff. Organizers say the contest could take time to build an audience.

“It would be profoundly arrogant to think that just because we have a heritage brand and a huge global audience for the European show, that we would walk in and demand it to be the same here,” said Martin Green, the European Broadcasting Union’s director of the Eurovision Song Contest. “Like any new thing, it needs to find its roots.”

Two previous attempts to take the competition to Asia were abandoned by the European Broadcasting Union, which owns Eurovision, and its partners in the region. A Eurovision spinoff in the United States, NBC’s American Song Contest, ran for one season in 2022.

The Asian edition kicking off on Saturday is far smaller than its European counterpart. Eurovision organizers said they were in talks with more countries to join future seasons. They include China, Japan and India, whose music industries have global reach.

“Bringing the world together through music is a fundamentally good idea,” Mr. Green said. “Europe shouldn’t keep it to itself.”

Here’s what we’re covering:

Politics: Geopolitics have long intruded on the European edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, but they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia. Read more ›

Voting process: Each artist will receive half their scores from professional juries in each country, and the other half from public voting on the Eurovision Asia website. Viewers are allowed to vote for artists from at least three other countries — not their own.

item.title: Geopolitics Looms Over Eurovision, but Not Its Asian Edition
item.description:
Geopolitics have long intruded on the Eurovision Song Contest. But they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia for the first time.

That was still true as of Saturday evening, as the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia was about to start in Bangkok.

Over the decades, Eurovision organizers have insisted that the contest is nonpolitical. Its organizers impose rules governing lyrics, political symbols and what can be broadcast. Even so, wars and diplomatic disputes have shaped who gets to sing, who stays home and what broadcasters are willing to air.

“Politics is why we watch Eurovision,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of the show at the University of Luxembourg.

Here are some examples of geopolitics bleeding into the European edition of the contest:

In 2009, less than a year after fighting a war with Russia, the former Soviet republic of Georgia planned to send a disco song called “We Don’t Wanna Put In” to Eurovision. Eurovision’s organizers said that the apparent dig at Vladimir Putin, then Russia’s prime minister, had to go. Georgia pulled out instead of changing it.

In 2017, Russia pulled out of the contest in Kyiv after Ukraine barred its singer from entering the country. And five years later, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Eurovision barred Russia altogether.

In 2024, the war in Gaza triggered mass protests over Israel’s participation. A bitter dispute over government influence on voting followed in 2025, and there were boycotts of the contest by five countries in 2026, the biggest crisis in Eurovision’s 70-year history.

The 11 Asian countries that sent artists to Saturday’s show have plenty of offstage geopolitical friction.

Cambodia, for example, is set to sing in Thailand’s capital less than a year after a border war between the two neighbors killed dozens and displaced hundreds of thousands. As fighting picked up last year, Cambodia withdrew its athletes from the Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, citing safety concerns.

But none of that has translated into a Eurovision controversy.

Mr. Vuletic said he expects Eurovision Asia to become a more visible platform for politics if the event continues over the next few years, drawing a wider audience and raising the stakes for countries taking part.

For now, some of Asia’s biggest powers are conspicuously absent from the lineup. Broadcasters from China, Japan and India discussed participating but did not sign up before the entry deadline, said Assaf Blecher, the contest’s executive producer. Pakistan and Indonesia are also absent.

China’s relations with Japan have been strained by a diplomatic dispute over Taiwan, which spilled into pop culture last year when Beijing canceled Japanese concerts and restricted films. China also has overlapping maritime claims in the South China Sea with the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia — countries that are all competing on Saturday.

Taiwan’s absence spares the organizers potentially sensitive decisions about names and flags. Beijing claims the self-governing island as its territory and opposes its treatment as an independent country. Such symbols have proved contentious at Eurovision, which in 2024 barred its audience from carrying Palestinian flags while permitting those of participating countries, including Israel.

Eurovision’s organizers have said the competition is “not a contest between governments.” But maintaining that distinction involves decisions about both what performers can sing and what broadcasters air.

The European contest’s rules prohibit political lyrics, speeches and gestures, and entrants may be asked to submit new songs or rewrite offending words. In 2024, organizers required Israel to change the title and lyrics of “October Rain,” which appeared to reference the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attacks. The song became “Hurricane.”

For all the trouble it can bring, the breadth of representation has also been part of Eurovision’s appeal since its founding in 1956, as an experiment in international television and an effort to bring Cold War Europe together. Bosnia and Herzegovina debuted in 1993 while Sarajevo, its capital, was under siege. Its singer, Fazla, told The New York Times in 2022 that he had escaped barefoot under sniper fire after his shoes became stuck in the mud.

“Eurovision is about representing your nation,” he said, “about giving yourself a platform to bring your story into the living rooms of normal people.”

Eurovision is not the only song contest to offer that platform. Russia revived the Cold War-era Intervision contest in 2025, after its exclusion from Eurovision over the invasion of Ukraine. It promoted the new competition as a showcase for what the Kremlin calls “traditional values.”

Vietnam’s Duc Phuc won that contest in Moscow.

On Saturday in Bangkok, another Vietnamese pop star, Toc Tien, will be first onstage at Eurovision Asia.

item.title: Asian love ballads test Eurovision’s winning song formula.
item.description:
When they sat down to plan the final show of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest in Asia, the organizers faced a challenge: How could they introduce variety when most of the entries were slow-paced love songs?

Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers.

“Europeans tend to prefer songs with a crescendo, a hook and a grand ending, but also a strong social message,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of contemporary Europe at the University of Luxembourg who is an authority on Eurovision.

“The audience doesn’t want to see an innocuous pop song,” he said.

Electro-pop and dance songs have featured heavily on the list of Eurovision winners over the past decade. In May, Bulgaria’s Dara won with “Bangaranga,” a dance-pop song inspired by her diagnosis with attention deficit hyperactive disorder. Nemo, from Switzerland, won in 2024 with an EDM opera about their nonbinary identity, while in 2018, Israel’s Netta won with “Toy,” a pop anthem about female independence.

Some countries hold a nationwide contest to select an artist and a song to represent them in Eurovision, while others leave the choice to Eurovision’s local broadcasting partner. Audiences in the Philippines voted for Carmelle in a televised competition, for example, while Vietnam Television chose Toc Tien.

The two are considered front-runners in the Asian edition, with their high-energy folk-pop songs about female empowerment.

Malaysia’s Aina Abdul, another early favorite, will showcase her powerful vocals in “Bluest Sky,” a ballad with an orchestral arrangement that is about a troubled relationship. The track is reminiscent of “Wasted Love,” an opera-techno song that won Austria the European title in 2025.

Pratik Himal Rai of Nepal, who got married this summer, said love was easy to sing about because it can be understood across borders and languages.

“It is love that holds the world together,” he said in an interview.

He will sing “Ananta Maya” in Nepali. Other Eurovision Asia artists blend English lyrics with their national languages.

In Europe, every winning song after 2022 has been in English. That year’s champion, Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra, sang in their own language on “Stefania,” a hip-hop track that interspersed a Ukrainian lullaby with rap verses and traditional woodwind instruments.

Winning songs tend to blend a country’s national instruments and musical motifs with internationally trendy pop, Mr. Vuletic said.

A traditional Bhutanese flute can be heard in “Lhayi Semo,” Nyendra’s love ballad. Monetrey’s “I Let You Go” uses a Cambodian bamboo xylophone and a tro, a string instrument played with a bow. A kulintang, a percussion instrument made of eight brass gongs, keeps the fast beat in Carmelle’s “Sobra-Sobra.”

item.title: Asia’s Eurovision Contest Is Missing Some Regional Heavyweights
item.description:
For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia has several notable absences.

For starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — won’t be there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, is absent.

That leaves some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.

As a result, the only large pop powerhouse in this contest is South Korea.

China’s absence is relatively simple to explain. Performers are entered by local broadcasters, and Eurovision has long had a messy relationship with China’s, which are heavily regulated and try to reflect the government’s social and political values. Mango TV once had a deal to broadcast the high-camp Eurovision to Chinese viewers, but Eurovision abruptly canceled it in 2018 after Mango TV censored acts whose performances featured gay themes. It also blurred rainbow flags in the performance arena.

Frank-Dieter Freiling, a former Eurovision official, said in an interview that such censorship was against Eurovision’s values and that the show’s organizers had historically barred broadcasters from airing the competition with delays.

It’s less clear why broadcasters from India, Pakistan, Japan and Indonesia are not participating. Assaf Blecher, Eurovision Asia’s executive producer, said that conversations with Chinese, Japanese and Indian broadcasters had not concluded in time. But he insisted that they “are knocking on our door.”

Not participating saves those countries the potential embarrassment of being the regional power that comes in last.

Just look to Europe, where Britain and Germany often perform badly at Eurovision. In this year’s show, Britain’s Look Mum No Computer placed last, scoring only one point, while Germany finished third from last. Whenever that happens, political commentators give interviews suggesting that the results reflect those countries’ poor standing across Europe.

item.title: Meet the Fans Who Traveled to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia
item.description:
Simon Robinson, one of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday, said that his history with the competition is nearly as long as its seven-decade run.

He was eight years old when he first watched it with his family in Yorkshire, England, when Britain's Mary Hopkin finished in second place behind Ireland’s Dana.

“I really liked the concept of bringing Europe together after the war,” said Mr. Robinson, 63, who now lives in Melbourne, Australia. He described the contest’s annual broadcast as a social activity for his family and neighbors.

“Eurovision helped to create the European identity,” he added.

Other fans had their own motivations for traveling to see the contest’s first Asian edition.

Some are Europeans living in Asia, on the hunt for nostalgia, while others are Americans who were eager to experience their first Eurovision.

Lee Hudson, an American television executive based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, said that he gets emotional when he talks about Eurovision, which he has watched since 2012.

“The only reason I know any music from European countries is because I heard them on Eurovision,” he said. “Eurovision Asia makes sense because the musical cultures are distinct.”

Mr. Hudson said he still listens to Loreen’s “Euphoria,” which won the competition for Sweden in 2012.

It was also the first Eurovision that Drew Andrea watched from his home in Sydney. A year later, he got a passport to fly to Sweden for the 2013 edition, and has attended every final since. Coming to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia was much more affordable, he said.

“Asia understands the brief — the kitschy costumes, the dance music,” he said.

His top picks among the Asian performers were the Philippines’ Carmelle and Vietnam’s Toc Tien. “I think they hit the nail on the head with the song, staging, costume and traditional elements,” he said.

Luca Cian, a professor of marketing at the University of Virginia who grew up in Italy, said that Eurovision built a global fan base by offering a shared cultural experience.

“Millions of people across Europe watch it at the same moment,” he said. “Families have watch parties with food and drinks. There are public discussions. Rituals create community.”

Carmen Chung, a British accountant, said she hijacked her family’s holiday in Bangkok to attend Eurovision Asia with her brother Garry Chung, a banker who lives in Hong Kong. “We were raised on Eurovision,” she said of their childhood in Yorkshire.

European acts, she said, tend to copy whatever style of music won the previous year. “This year, because there are no expectations, everyone has just done their own thing,” she said. She and her brother said they were rooting for Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, a beatboxing group that will perform an a cappella love song.

Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said that about half of the tickets for Saturday’s final were purchased by “super fans” from outside Asia. Organizers have kept the inaugural show modest, with 11 participating countries and a 5,000-seat venue.

Mr. Andrea said he didn’t mind the small scale.

“I’m O.K. with humble beginnings as long as it keeps growing every year,” he said.

item.title: A Mexican Artist Sang Some of His Hits. Authorities Stopped the Show, Then Arrested Him.
item.description:
A popular Mexican singer’s concert was halted on Friday night because he performed songs considered to be glorifying cartel culture, making him the latest and most high-profile artist to be ensnared in a government crackdown on the genre known as narcocorridos.

He was later arrested by the federal authorities in relation to an unrelated investigation.

Gabito Ballesteros, 27, whose songs have billions of streams, was performing at a fair in Querétaro State in central Mexico when authorities escorted him off the stage.

Before the show, his set list was reviewed and approved by state officials and event organizers, according to a statement issued by the fair. Songs that glorified criminal activities were explicitly excluded, in accordance with state regulations, the fair said.

Last year, the state joined several other states and municipalities throughout Mexico that effectively prohibit the public performance of so-called narcocorridos, a version of traditional Mexican ballads that celebrate drug cartels instead of historic events and everyday life. Violations were punishable with fines or even jail time.

The actions — and the genre itself — have sparked much debate in Mexico, which has been wrestling with both the effects of organized crime, particularly amid pressure from the Trump administration to crack down on cartels, and its identity as defined through popular culture. The discussion also has became a referendum on free speech.

On Friday night, Mr. Ballesteros performed an unauthorized song and local authorities took him offstage to remind him of his prior agreement, the fair said. When he returned, the fair said Mr. Ballesteros started to perform another unauthorized song, “AMG.” The 2022 hit, which references the luxurious lifestyles and fancy cars of cartel members, has nearly one billion streams on Spotify.

The authorities then halted the concert. In videos shared online by fans, Mr. Ballesteros did not immediately leave the stage.

During a live transmission on his Instagram page later, Mr. Ballesteros showed himself sitting in his pickup truck surrounded by police. He said he changed the order of his songs based on the crowd’s feedback and that he was not going to perform any prohibited songs. He also said that his security guards had been detained and that he was not going to get out of the pickup.

Mr. Ballesteros was arrested by state police early Saturday morning and handed over to federal authorities, according to federal booking records.

The federal attorney general’s office said in a statement that it had opened an investigation into the potential illegal possession of a firearm, which is a federal crime, as well as disobedience and resistance. Mr. Ballesteros was among five people arrested.

Federal prosecutors said that five people entered a pickup truck, inside of which a firearm was spotted. They said that a handgun, two magazines and 34 rounds of ammunition were seized. They said that are investigating whether a permit exists for the firearm and to determine “the legal status” of the people in custody.

“In the state of Querétaro, the performance of music that glorifies criminal activity is prohibited at public events, as part of a zero-tolerance policy toward content that promotes violence or organized crime,” the fair said. “Local legislation stipulates the immediate suspension of such events,” fines of nearly $54,000 and banning repeat offenders.

The performance was stopped “to protect the public, ensure order and uphold the law,” the fair said. “It is not directed against the music itself, nor any specific artist.”

In a statement posted Saturday night on social media, Mr. Ballesteros’ agent issued an apology.

“We acknowledge that this was an error in judgment and sincerely regret the situation that occurred,” it read. “It was never our intention to cause controversy or discomfort, nor to show any disrespect toward the authorities or institutions.”

While there have been past attempts to ban narcocorridos in Mexico, experts have said that this latest crackdown is the strongest. President Claudia Sheinbaum has publicly positioned herself against the genre, but she had rejected flat-out bans and instead started a government-run music contest for more wholesome lyrics that awarded record label deals to the winners.

Mr. Ballesteros is not the first artist to get in trouble for performing narcocorridos recently — it happened to another artist in February in Sinaloa, a state ravaged by cartel violence — but he is certainly the most high-profile.

Experts have raised concerns about recent backsliding on freedom of expression in Mexico. Politicians and officials have increasingly weaponized the country’s laws to sue, fine and harass critics and journalists, according to press rights groups tracking legal cases. Human rights groups worried about the Mexican government’s past attempts to fine media outlets for allegedly false information.

Jorge Álvarez Máynez, a former presidential candidate and the head of a political party opposing Ms. Sheinbaum’s governing party, said he sent a complaint on Saturday to Mexico’s National Human Rights Commission about Mr. Ballesteros’s treatment.

“It’s not about combating the expressions of pop culture that emerge from everyday life in Mexico,” he said. “What needs to be combated is organized crime, violence and impunity.”

item.title: A Grizzly Known as ‘the Boss’ Rules Banff Park, and Draws a Crowd
item.description:
To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park he is grizzly bear 122. But to everyone who lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, and many of its 4.5 million annual visitors, he is the Boss.

He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect. He has shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and snacked on a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his 2,000-square-kilometer territory.

Most of all, the Boss has become Canada’s 700-pound celebrity bear king. When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, “bear jams” swiftly follow. His battles with a rival bear known as Split Lip are legendary. (He caused the split lip.) His annual awakening from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.

Galleries in Banff and neighboring Canmore ship giant photos of him worldwide. His image appears on fridge magnets, T-shirts and tote bags. A local restaurant is named for him, its main dining room dominated by a scrap metal sculpture of the bear.

But despite his fearsome demeanor, enhanced by four-inch claws, few bear experts consider the Boss a threat to park visitors or residents. Rather, they fear his celebrity and the legions of fans it have created, may be the biggest threat to his life and his dominance.

Among those concerned about the cost of celebrity is Paul Kalra, a gas station owner and nature photographer who drew attention to the bear more than 20 years ago with photos in a local newspaper and is widely credited with naming him.

“Give him a break,” Mr. Kalra said, sitting at a table at the restaurant in his service station in Dead Man’s Flats. “Even the movie stars that are most famous, they go incognito with sunglasses when they go to have a burger, you know? I want same thing for the Boss.”

About 75 grizzly bears roam the mountains, rivers and valleys of Banff National Park’s 6,641 square kilometers. How the Boss came to stand out is a matter of geography as much as his size and legends. His home turf overlaps with the park’s main tourist gateway.

Grizzlies can, of course, be dangerous. This month conservation officers in British Columbia killed a female grizzly and her three cubs after DNA connected them to a fatal attack on a women and her daughter.

But although the Boss strolled into Canmore, a former coal mining town just east of the park three years ago, apparently looking for crab apples, David Laskin, a Parks Canada wildlife ecologist said the danger that most grizzlies pose is overstated.

“A lot of people rob themselves of enjoyable experiences in the wilderness because they’re scared of bears,” he said at a park picnic table festooned with signs warning against feeding animals. “Bears need to be respected. Getting close to a bear: There’s a risk for you but also for the bear especially. We don’t want to put bears in a situation where they have to defend themselves.”

The Boss has eaten other bears, but he and all of Banff’s grizzlies are largely vegetarians, Dr. Laskin said. Berries, roots and other plant materials make up about 90 percent of their diet. Maintaining 700 pounds on a berry-heavy diet forces grizzlies to range widely and eat vigorously. The Boss can put away about 200,000 buffaloberries a day, Dr. Laskin said. When he wore a tracking collar for most of 2012, he traveled about 1,400 kilometers in search of food.

“They’re actually surprisingly delicate in how they pull berries from shrubs, from branches,” he said. “They’ll use their claws and they’ll just pull a branch to their mouths and just kind of nibble off the berries”

Locals are quick to volunteer Boss stories. Bill Hunt, the former natural resources conservation manager at Banff, had an encounter about three years ago as he was packing to move from his Canmore house.

“I was packing up the U-Haul and he came walking right up the street past my house, probably 12 feet away,” Mr. Hunt said. “That’s why he got that name. He could have gone around, he could have gone down the power line, 20 feet below the house. But he came right down the middle of the road — big white claws hanging over the front.”

Mr. Kalra won’t profit off the Boss by selling photos of the bear, but he displays some at his service station. Mr. Kalra, who was born in India and moved to moved to Canmore in 1989, said that, like Mr. Hunt, he has always been struck by the bear’s indifference toward humans.

“The biggest thing is his gentleness and his respect towards the people,” Mr. Kalra said. “He has never done any harm to anyone. And that means more to me than anything else.”

Under the park’s bear management plan, the Boss is “habituated,” a category for bears that don’t really care about people as long as they are left alone.

That said, when the park’s network of trail cams, sightings and paw prints suggests that he’s headed toward Banff, Canmore or campgrounds, park workers gently shoo him in another direction while clearing visitors from his path. (It’s unclear if plans to eliminate 500 jobs at Parks Canada will affect that program.)

Despite the large influx of visitors into Banff, serious bear incidents remain rare, Mr. Hunt said. They generally involve “wary” bears, the vast majority of the population, in remote parts of the park.

“When you’re encountering a wary bear that hadn’t seen a person in three months, both sides are scared and terrified, and the bigger animal wins,” Mr. Hunt said. “It’s often just a quick swat and then they realize what they’ve encountered and they take off.”

But the most worrisome bears, Mr. Hunt said, are those that decide that exploiting human activity — from garbage to bird feeders and fruit trees — beats looking for berries.

“It’s very subtle, but it’s a very big change,” Mr. Hunt said. “That is when bears become dangerous.”

In addition to the signs ordering park visitors not to feed animals, Canmore and Banff have strict rules around garbage and programs to replace fruit trees.

Now in his mid-20s, the Boss is getting old for a bear, prompting speculation about whether he will emerge from hibernation in the spring.

Earlier this year, Dr. Laskin got up close with him. The Boss was found in a trap set for another study bear. “We thought he was too smart for that,” he said. The Boss was sedated, examined and fitted for a collar that soon fell off, most likely in a fight.

Grizzlies typically peak physically at about 10 and then gradually shrink, but Dr. Laskin said that there’s no sign of that in the Boss.

His teeth, however, are “worn, but that’s not unusual for a bear his age.”

His odor? “Not a good smell.”

When asked about the Boss’s fur, Dr. Laskin demurred at first.

“I shouldn’t make any comments about the tactile characteristics of grizzly bears,” he said, apparently concerned that some visitors might treat the park as a petting zoo.

Then he relented.

“Their name comes from the characteristics of their fur, where you have a soft coat with guard hairs that extend beyond that coat,” he said. “They’re a bit lighter than the rest of the coat, and it gives that grizzled appearance. And, yeah, they’re soft.”

item.title: In Europe, an Emboldened Iran Contributes to a Sense of Anxiety
item.description:
On Veterans Day this past week, President Trump declared that his decision to go to war with Iran had been a complete success.

“When this conflict is over, and it will be soon,” he said, speaking on a blustery morning from Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington, “the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place.”

That is not how it feels in Europe.

A growing number of attempted terrorist attacks across the continent and in Britain, including a foiled plot against a major American military base, arson attacks on Jewish community sites and cyberattacks that raised temperatures in refrigerators and blood banks are rattling national security officials and unnerving the public. Many have been attributed to Iran or to proxies acting on its behalf.

The sense of global unease was heightened when the U.S. government grounded all air travel for hours on Friday in what officials later said was a technical issue.

European residents had already grown frustrated before the most recent round of turmoil. The economic consequences of the war that Mr. Trump and the Israeli government started against Iran in February have piled up: Gas prices are higher because of disruptions of oil deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz. Groceries cost more. Heating homes in winter has become far less affordable.

And in recent weeks, the effect has grown darker as security officials have accused Iran or its proxies of conducting a series of terrorism-related plots. In September, U.S. prosecutors say, an Iraqi man, an Iranian operative and a senior operative for an Iran proxy group in a New York jail plotted to attack R.A.F. Fairford, an air base in England used by American bombers. They did not succeed, but the effort prompted a major security incident.

In October, grocery store refrigerators in France were hit by a cyberattack that rotted millions of dollars’ worth of food, a tactic repeated this month in some supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. Several French blood banks were also hacked. On Monday, France accused Iran of orchestrating the refrigerator attacks in its country, calling it a large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage.

From the beginning, political leaders across Europe were eager to avoid being dragged into Mr. Trump’s war.

Officials in Spain, Germany, France and Britain all declared they would not take part in America’s offensive attacks on Tehran, even as some host American military bases. Despite that, they appear to have become collateral damage as Iran seeks to show the consequences if Mr. Trump resumes aggressive actions.

“Iran is signaling very clearly to the Europeans that if the U.S. resumes the war, Europe is going to also become part of the target list for counter escalation,” said Ellie Geranmayeh, a Middle East and North Africa expert at the European Council on Foreign Relations. “It’s a sign of Iran’s desperation that they are trying to drag the Europeans into this global pain.”

Gen. Roly Walker, the chief of the general staff in Britain, told troops last month that “there is extreme jeopardy in the world at the moment,” adding that “very soon, the political leaders of this country will start to have a frank conversation with the citizens of this country, about just what is going on and where the risk lies.”

Of course Iran is not the only source of threats in Europe. Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine has led to an increasing number of sabotage operations, including the jamming of aviation signals over Sweden, drones flying over Danish and Belgian airports and the smuggling of explosives into Poland in cans of corn. Western officials accuse Russia of trying to undermine European support for Ukraine.

Not all of the disruption has a clear origin. This past week, bomb threats were emailed to thousands of schools in Italy, forcing hundreds of them to be evacuated. That came after planes in Italy, Poland, Spain and elsewhere were grounded or diverted because of bomb threats that turned out to be hoaxes. Officials have not determined who was behind the threats.

As of Saturday, American officials said the decision to ground all flights in the country for several hours, which also affected flights at London’s Heathrow Airport and other international hubs, did not appear to be the result of a cyberattack. Officials at the U.S. Department of Transportation said they issued the temporary ban on flights because of failures in the system’s “antiquated, legacy communications equipment.”

But intelligence officials are increasingly concerned about retaliation by Iran’s government in response to the attacks by the United States and Israel.

In his annual threat update last month, Ken McCallum, the director general of MI5, said that Iran has shifted its ambitions to attack “harder targets, like military sites.”

On Sept. 27, the police apprehended five British men as they drove three vans near R.A.F. Fairford, the air base that hosted American bombers flying sorties to Iran. Two individuals were later charged with national security offenses over the plot, with prosecutors saying they believed it was orchestrated by a man believed to be working for the Iranian state.

Iran has forcefully denied any involvement in the Fairford plot.

More light was shed on the plot in a federal grand jury indictment unsealed in New York this past week, which provides a window into Iran’s efforts to conduct what the document calls the “European terrorist attacks.”

The indictment says the attempted attacks were directed by Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a commander of Kataib Hezbollah, an Iraqi militia that is one of Iran’s most powerful proxies. According to investigators, Mr. al-Saadi helped plan and initiate the Fairford attack while in prison in New York, where he had been charged with plotting attacks on Jewish institutions in Europe, including London.

After the foiled attack at Fairford, the United States quickly withdrew all 12 of its B-1 Air Force bombers from the air base. Officials said they had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the installation.

As many as a dozen U.S. military aircraft were also evacuated from R.A.F. Mildenhall in England this past week, with officials saying they had detected an Iran-backed drone plot.

Security officials and analysts said the Iran-backed plots in Britain were likely prompted by the heavy presence of American forces and planes that were used in the attacks on Iran at the beginning of the war.

Keir Starmer, who at the time was the British prime minister, did not join the war with Iran and blocked the United States from using its British bases for offensive attacks. But after initial hesitation, he allowed what he called “defensive” bombing campaigns by American forces against Iran, saying they were necessary to protect British and allied interests in that region.

Soon after that decision, the Joint Terrorism Analysis Center in Britain raised the terrorism threat level to its second-highest level: “SEVERE — an attack is highly likely.” At the time, officials cited “a series of arson attacks and incidents against British Jews and opponents of the Iranian regime,” along with other incidents.

In recent months, Iran appears to have broadened its targets to include countries — like France — which did not host American military forces used in the war. The U.S. State Department has issued “Level 2” travel advisories for many European countries, urging travelers to “exercise increased caution” because of the threat of terrorism.

Viktorija Rusinaite, the director of research and analysis at the European Center of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats in Helsinki, Finland, said the targets of Iran’s terrorism threats have changed in the past nine months.

Before the war with Iran began in February, Ms. Rusinaite said, Iran tended to initiate attacks on Iranian dissidents and opposition figures living abroad, along with American and Israeli targets. Now, she said, the Iranian security system appears more willing to go after European targets more broadly.

“This seems to be changing right now,” she said. Before the war, she added, “they would see, for example, opposition or free media as a threat to regime survival. They’re now seeing that some of the European countries might threaten regime survival as well.”

Ms. Rusinaite said it was also possible that cooperation between Russia and Iran, including trade in military weapons and expertise, could “strengthen Iranian hybrid threat capabilities and might make things more complicated for European security officials.”

item.title: The Italianization of Europe
item.description:
When I first moved to Rome, I spent my time living in the past.

At the turn of the century, I drifted through a vintage postcard of postwar Italy: old women sitting around tables they had dragged into the street, old men playing cards in caps, cats arching their backs on the hoods of snub-nosed Fiats.

As newspapers filled with talk of Silvio Berlusconi, a media mogul with ambitions and appetites worthy of a Roman emperor, my meanderings inevitably took me toward Tiber Island, a sliver of land in the middle of the river that divides Rome.

An ancient bridge on the island’s left bank had a strange statue of weather-beaten faces positioned back-to-back as if they couldn’t stand one another. The heads rose out of the shared torso of a square pillar and represented Janus, Rome’s god of the past and future, the deity of transitions and change.

Back then, I didn’t see the change around me, but now, more than a quarter-century later, after spending decades reporting on Italian politics and changes across Europe, I have come to understand that I was living in the future.

In the time since, I have seen an Italianization of politics all around the continent, with coalitions of small parties resulting in instability, with fed-up voters desperate for new saviors. But more than anything, I have seen — in Britain, France, Germany — countries following the Italian model by allowing the far right into the political mainstream.

Spain, where I’m now The New York Times’s bureau chief, will hold elections this month. Polls show the far-right party Vox — which largely feeds on anti-Muslim, anti-migrant and anti-E.U. sentiment — is likely to join the mainstream conservative party in a new government. The current left-wing government led by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, a beacon for Europe’s liberals, is trying to mobilize supporters by warning against the regressive politics Vox represents. Some of his officials invoke the dictatorship of Francisco Franco.

But I keep thinking back to Mr. Berlusconi.

Soon before I arrived in Italy as a student in the late 1990s, Mr. Berlusconi, who many see as creating the mold for President Trump, first brought in “the fascists,” as he called the far right, to help govern with him. Berlusconi’s calculus was purely political. He needed the votes to form a winning coalition in 1994 and to gain power, not least to protect his vast business interests from prosecutors.

His decision broke a major postwar taboo. Mr. Berlusconi eventually claimed credit for upending the political establishment that had governed Italy since the end of World War II. Those mainstream politicians had made something of a backroom deal to keep the fascist forces descended from Mussolini, the dictator who had nearly destroyed the country, away from power. Mr. Berlusconi clearly understood he had violated that pact. “We let them into the government in ’94 and we legitimized them,” he said.

In Mr. Berlusconi’s eyes, he was neutering, not normalizing, the “fascists.” Their alliance was an act of what Italian politicians taught me was “Romanization,” the age-old process by which any “barbarian,” no matter how ferocious and dangerous, could be tamed by the transactional nature, and irresistible gravity, of the Roman swamp. “In Italy, you can never have a revolution, because we all know each other,” went one famous phrase.

Plus, this particular swamp came with powerful guardrails created after World War II to prevent another strongman like Mussolini and, as time went on, added restrictions imposed by the European Union.

Those limits, and Italy’s deeply embedded conservatism and resistance to radicalism that could threaten the jealously guarded wealth — and real estate — of its people, produced a paradox: Italians were apt to let a party try out newfangled ideas — because nobody really expected anything to change.

It’s not for nothing that the national motto often seemed to be an observation from the great novel “The Leopard” by Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa. “Everything must change so that everything can stay the same,” a prince famously puts it, or, in another translation, “If we want things to stay as they are, things will have to change.”

Italy’s insulation from change was exactly what made it a safe space as a political laboratory. Over the years, I had seen no shortage of experiments — megalomaniacal mogul turned face of the nation, a government run by proudly unprepared Internet-native populists, save-the-day technocrats. Whenever it seemed things were going off the rails, the flexible Italian system would call time on the experiment — and new elections were held. The infamous Italian instability was actually a way to preserve stability.

But one experiment seemed more significant, and sticky, than the others, and that was Mr. Berlusconi’s decision, out of political necessity or — in his telling — civic duty, to bring the far right into power.

In the decades after Mr. Berlusconi’s short-lived 1994 government, the neo-fascist leaders who had joined it inched away from the margins and their taboos.

They distanced themselves from Mussolini and decried the Holocaust. Eventually, Giorgia Meloni, a teenager reared in the victimization culture of neo-Fascism, became a party leader, government minister and, during my time as the Rome bureau chief for The Times, the country’s most popular politician.

I had watched her political rise over decades, and when we sipped spritzes together in a Sardinian courtyard shortly before her election as prime minister in 2022, she insisted she led a mainstream conservative party.

I asked her whether she agreed with what she had simply called “the historical judgment” that Mussolini was bad for Italy — even if one subtracted the usual neo-fascist caveats that he had erred in allying with Hitler, in enacting racial laws and in almost destroying Italy and Europe by getting involved in World War II. With some prodding she even uttered a quiet “yeah.”

Ms. Meloni’s election seemed the culmination of something. I wasn’t sure then if, like Janus, I was looking forward or backward. I wasn’t sure if Mr. Berlusconi’s “Romanization” bet had succeeded in sapping neo-fascist forces or if it had backfired spectacularly and breathed them new life, bringing the world back a century.

But it mattered, I thought. Even if Italy seemed inoculated against the risks of its own political experiments, I wasn’t convinced that a lab leak to a world with fewer antibodies would not be a dangerous thing.

Since then, Ms. Meloni has become the Italian Republic’s longest-serving prime minister, likely to serve out her five-year term ahead of elections next year. Her fiscal and foreign policies are essentially those of a mainstream conservative. She has not wavered in her support for Ukraine. An initial effort to become Europe’s bridge to Mr. Trump failed. She has clearly taken the side of the European Union, on which Italy depends for financial aid, another illustration of the continent’s guardrails against rogue nationalism.

The establishment has gone from fearing Ms. Meloni to embracing her. The European Union values her as a partner and has moved closer to her positions on immigration.

After Ms. Meloni gave remarks to a gala held by Italy’s Foreign Press Association in 2025, during which she called the evening “an occasion to know one another,” she sat for more than an hour on a couch in the corner as reporters from around the world took turns talking to her, but mostly taking selfies.

At the end, I watched with disbelief from the back of the room as they gave her a bouquet of flowers, and Ms. Meloni danced with some of the reporters to “Billie Jean.” It was a raging success for Ms. Meloni, whose international normalization campaign was going splendidly. On the way out, I caught her eye. She gave me a look as if to say she couldn’t believe how well it had gone either.

Ahead of Italy’s elections, critics are arguing that Ms. Meloni hasn’t done much in government. While some still worry that she might feel bolder about taking the country farther right if she wins next year, they cannot, in any credible way, accuse her of governing Italy as a fascist or authoritarian.

As important as how she has governed is the very fact that she’s governed at all. She’s shown Europe’s hard-right forces — similarly inspired by neo-Fascism, but in countries without Italy’s kind of restraints — that they can win. It’s hard not to see that leaders of parties once seen as extremist — Marine Le Pen in France, Alice Weidel in Germany, Santiago Abascal in Spain — owe her a debt.

She had made any lingering neo-fascist odor much less offensive.

“For us it would happen the same,” Carlos Flores, a member of the Spanish Parliament and a prominent voice in the nationalist party Vox, told me soon after I arrived in Spain. He looked to Ms. Meloni as a model, envisioning a Spain that protected its culture and traditions, embraced nationalism and closed its doors to immigrants.

“We will carry out a portion of our program,” he said, and like he hoped Ms. Meloni would do, “We will wait until people give us the sufficient mandate to carry out the rest.”

As he envisioned that new, or maybe old, Spain over coffee in Valencia, I thought back to the Janus statues on the Tiber Island in Rome and to what my life in Italy had taught me. The land of the past often pointed toward our future.
